name: BitBang (bitbang-cli)
popularity: 350 stars, 27 forks, 3 watchers. Small but growing project with an active whitepaper/companion repo (richlegrand/bitbang). No major public adoption evidence beyond GitHub stars.
maturity: Actively developed (218 commits on main, CI tests passing badge). Recent project (README references 2024/2025-era peer-to-peer/WebRTC design). No obvious red flags for the client, but the rendezvous/introducer server is a hosted proprietary service (bitba.ng) whose source is NOT in this repo (repo only contains cmd/, internal/, tests/ -- no server directory).
client_requirements: Single static Go binary (curl | sh installer or `go build`), no admin/root privileges, no TAP/TUN interfaces. Client establishes an end-to-end encrypted, peer-to-peer WebRTC connection directly to the browser or another `bitbang connect` client; the WebRTC signaling/rendezvous is handled by the bitba.ng server which merely 'introduces the two ends, then steps aside.' This materially changes requirements versus classic reverse tunnels: no persistent inbound listener is needed on our side, but it also means we cannot easily front it with our own control-plane/API since the matchmaking server logic is closed/hosted, not part of this OSS repo.
server_requirements: The public bitba.ng rendezvous/signaling server's source is not published in this repo (only client code: cmd/, internal/). No visible TypeScript/JavaScript server package despite being marketed as simple/'no client to install' -- the CLI itself is Go, not JS. There is no documented HTTP REST API for programmatic tunnel registration; it is a WebRTC signaling service, not a config-file or API-driven reverse-tunnel server we could self-host and wire into our own control plane.
server_language: Unknown/undisclosed (rendezvous/signaling server not in this repo; likely Go given ecosystem, but not open-sourced here)
has_programmable_api: false -- no rendezvous/signaling server source or API surface is published in this repo; only a Go CLI client exists.
viability_notes: Client-side requirements are excellent (single Go binary, no root, no TUN, WebRTC-based), but the whole value proposition depends on a closed/hosted rendezvous server whose source and control-plane API are not available in this repo, making it impossible to self-host with our own SvelteKit-driven registration API as required.

name: hypertunnel
popularity: 271 stars, 50 forks, 4 watchers. Published to npm as `hypertunnel`. Moderate adoption for a niche TCP relay tool circa 2018-2019; no major current production use found.
maturity: Lerna/yarn-workspaces monorepo, Travis CI (an old CI system), 71 commits. README explicitly states 'Status: ... certain things could be improved and battle-hardened' and that programmatic usage 'comes with no warranty as internals might change.' The task context notes the public hosted server (hypertunnel.ga) is down; the project shows no recent activity/releases, effectively unmaintained.
client_requirements: CLI usable via `npx hypertunnel --port 8080` or global npm install. No TAP/TUN, no admin/root needed for the client (just a Node.js/npx-capable environment) -- straightforward for our use case as long as Node is available on the client host.
server_requirements: Server source IS available in-repo as the `hypertunnel-tcp-relay` package (Node/JS), built on `node-tcp-relay`, fully self-hostable. It is a generic TCP relay (not HTTP-only) supporting multi-client self-service tunnels similar to localtunnel. However, there is no documented REST/HTTP control-plane API for programmatic tunnel registration; the README explicitly says internals are 'not properly documented' and points to the test suite as the only guide to programmatic use.
has_programmable_api: Partial/true -- JavaScript (Node.js) server package exists and can theoretically be embedded/driven programmatically as a library, but there's no stable, documented HTTP REST API; it's undocumented internal APIs only, and the project itself calls this unsupported/unstable.
viability_notes: The only candidate in this batch with a genuinely open-source JS/Node server, which is attractive, but it is effectively abandoned (old CI, undocumented/unstable internals, dead public instance) and offers no real control-plane API -- high integration risk for a production hosted service.

name: Portal (portal-tunnel)
popularity: 269 stars, 28 forks, 1 watcher. Tagged in anderspitman/awesome-tunneling. Includes VS Code extension, Claude/Cursor plugin integrations, and a frontend/docs site -- signs of an emerging but real ecosystem.
maturity: Very actively developed: 1,653 commits on main, CI badge passing, dedicated docs site (SvelteKit-based docs under docs/), llms.txt, plugins for coding agents. This looks like the most actively maintained project in the batch.
client_requirements: Single Go binary (portal-tunnel CLI / SDK), no TAP/TUN, no admin/root privileges required -- backend makes outbound-only reverse connections to the relay (no inbound listener, no elevated ports needed on the client side).
server_requirements: Relay server source fully available (Go), self-hostable (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, config.toml). Crucially it exposes a genuine HTTP control-plane API under `/sdk/*`: `POST /sdk/register/challenge`, `POST /sdk/register`, `GET /sdk/connect`, `POST /sdk/renew`, `POST /sdk/unregister` -- i.e., programmatic lease/tunnel registration, renewal, and teardown via REST-style calls (auth via SIWE/secp256k1 signature challenge + JWT access tokens). Also supports optional dedicated TCP/UDP port allocation.
server_language: Go (relay-server binary); client/SDK also Go, with a `sdk/` directory for embedding.
has_programmable_api: true -- Go relay server exposes an HTTP/JSON control-plane API (`/sdk/register`, `/sdk/connect`, `/sdk/renew`, `/sdk/unregister`) suitable for driving tunnel lifecycle programmatically from an external app (e.g., our SvelteKit backend could call this API directly or shell out to the SDK).
viability_notes: Strongest overall fit among the Go options: self-hostable open-source relay with a real HTTP control-plane for programmatic registration/renewal/teardown, no TAP/TUN, no root, single-binary client, and clearly the most actively maintained project surveyed. Docks a point only because the control-plane is Go/JSON rather than a first-class TypeScript SDK, and the protocol (SIWE-signed registration, keyless TLS, QUIC) is more complex than a typical simple REST integration.

name: reverse-tunnel (rtun)
popularity: 244 stars, 39 forks, 11 watchers. Docker images published (snsinfu/rtun, snsinfu/rtun-server). Modest but respectable following for a single-purpose tool.
maturity: 75 commits, GitHub Actions CI passing, CHANGELOG.md maintained, releases published. Reasonably healthy but low commit velocity; no obvious red flags, appears stable/finished rather than actively evolving.
client_requirements: Single Go binary agent (`rtun`), no TAP/TUN, no admin/root needed for normal ports (root/setcap only required if binding to privileged ports like 443 on the server side). Config is a local YAML file (`rtun.yml`) specifying the gateway URL, auth key, and per-port forwards.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go, `server/` directory), self-hostable, communicates over WebSocket (can sit behind an HTTPS reverse proxy like Caddy for TLS). Configuration is entirely YAML config-file driven (`rtun-server.yml` listing authorized agents/auth_keys and whitelisted ports) -- there is no HTTP REST API for dynamically registering/managing agents or tunnels at runtime; adding an agent requires editing the server config file (and presumably restarting/reloading).
has_programmable_api: false -- no REST/HTTP control-plane; agent registration and port whitelisting are static YAML config, not programmatically manageable via an API.
viability_notes: Solid, simple, self-hostable Go reverse tunnel over WebSocket with an admin-free, TUN-free client -- meets all hard client constraints -- but it is strictly config-file driven with no API/control-plane, so our SvelteKit app would need to template and reload YAML files rather than call an HTTP API to register tunnels.

name: chiSSL
popularity: 195 stars, 8 forks, 4 watchers (repo now lives under the 'unblocked' GitHub org, formerly NextChapterSoftware). Modest star count but polished docs site, Homebrew tap, and one-line server installer suggest real production usage internally at NextChapterSoftware/Unblocked.
maturity: 37 commits but clearly a mature, feature-rich fork/successor of chisel (jpillora/chisel lineage), with a full documentation site (mkdocs, unblocked.github.io/chissl), Homebrew formula, versioned installer script (v2.0), and CI. No obvious abandonment signals; presents as a maintained internal tool open-sourced by the company.
client_requirements: Single static Go binary client (Homebrew install or prebuilt release binary), no TAP/TUN interfaces, no admin/root privileges. Client config can be a simple CLI invocation or a YAML profile file at `$HOME/.chissl/profile.yaml`.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go, `server/` directory), self-hostable with a one-line installer script, automatic TLS via Let's Encrypt domain or custom certs. Explicitly documents 'REST API and web dashboard' as a headline feature, with a published OpenAPI spec (openapi-public.yaml) and Redoc-rendered API reference at unblocked.github.io/chissl/api/. Supports SQLite (default) or PostgreSQL for persistence, admin/user RBAC, API tokens, and optional SSO -- this is the most API/control-plane-complete option in the batch.
has_programmable_api: true -- Go server exposes a documented REST API (OpenAPI/Redoc spec published) plus a web dashboard, covering tunnel/listener management, multicast tunnels, users, and API tokens -- directly usable for programmatic registration from an external app.
viability_notes: Best fit overall: fully self-hostable Go server with a real, documented REST API (OpenAPI spec + dashboard) for managing tunnels/listeners/tokens programmatically, and a client that is a single admin-free, TUN-free binary. Only caveats are its relatively small star count and its being a fork of chisel with a smaller community than the upstream project, but functionally it directly satisfies every hard requirement.

name: srv.us
language: Go (backend); no client code needed (uses stock OpenSSH)
popularity: 180 stars, 15 forks, 1 watcher. Repository now canonically at xmit-co/srv.us (redirect from pcarrier/srvus). Backed by a live production hosted service (srv.us) with GitHub/GitLab identity integration and a Discord support community.
maturity: 84 commits, actively described as a running production service with systemd/certbot renewal automation and documented plans to scale (open issue tracked). No red flags; simple and stable, low commit churn because scope is intentionally minimal.
client_requirements: No client software to install at all -- uses the user's existing OpenSSH client (`ssh srv.us -R 1:localhost:3000`), so effectively the simplest possible client: no TAP/TUN, no admin/root, no binary to distribute, only an SSH keypair. Extremely attractive from a 'zero install' standpoint, but it is not something our own hosted server binary can control -- it depends on their specific SSH-based multiplexed server.
server_requirements: Server ('backend/', Go) is open source and self-hostable in principle (systemd service + certbot for TLS), but it is architected as a bespoke SSH server that maps `-R` port-forward requests to public HTTPS subdomains keyed off the client's SSH key/GitHub identity -- there is no REST/HTTP API for programmatic tunnel registration; registration is implicit via the SSH protocol itself (an SSH session *is* the registration action).
has_programmable_api: false -- no HTTP control-plane; interaction model is purely 'establish an SSH -R session', which is hard to drive/manage from a SvelteKit backend without shelling out to `ssh` and parsing terminal output.
viability_notes: Exceptionally simple for a human running one command, and the server is technically open source, but the total absence of any REST/control-plane API (registration is baked into raw SSH port-forward semantics) makes it a poor fit for programmatic per-tunnel management from our SvelteKit app.

name: bore (jkuri/bore)
popularity: 163 stars, 18 forks, 5 watchers. Hosted public instance at bore.digital. Reasonably well known within the ngrok-alternative space (tagged localtunnel/ngrok/ssh topics) though smaller than the unrelated Rust project also named 'bore' (ekzhang/bore).
maturity: 83 commits, MIT license copyright through 2023, prebuilt release binaries available. No obvious signs of abandonment but modest, steady-state activity; not under heavy active development.
client_requirements: Prebuilt single Go binary or build-from-source, no TAP/TUN, no admin/root required. Connects out to the bore-server via SSH-secured tunnel and needs only CLI flags (server, port, local port).
server_requirements: Server source fully available in-repo (Go, `server/` directory), self-hostable via environment variables (BORE_DOMAIN, BORE_HTTPADDR, BORE_SSHADDR) which generate a YAML config file (`~/bore/bore-server.yaml`) on first run. No documented HTTP REST API for programmatic tunnel registration/management -- clients request tunnels directly via the CLI protocol (custom IDs, custom remote ports), not via any separate control-plane endpoint we could call from our app.
has_programmable_api: false -- config/env-var driven server with no REST/HTTP control-plane; tunnel creation happens implicitly when a bore client connects, not through an API we call.
viability_notes: Meets the hard client constraints well (single binary, no root, no TUN) and the server is open source and simple to self-host, but there's no programmatic registration API -- our glue code would need to spawn/manage bore client processes per tunnel rather than call a control-plane.

name: vgrok
popularity: 153 stars, 5 forks, 1 watcher. Published to npm as `@styfle/vgrok`. Small hobby-scale project by a well-known developer (styfle, of Vercel/Next.js fame), but limited independent adoption evidence.
maturity: Only 31 commits; README frames it as designed for 'quick local development' and lists unresolved caveats (45-min sandbox timeout on Hobby plans, single-region iad1 only, no multi-connection support, noisy logs) -- signals of an early-stage/experimental tool rather than production-hardened infrastructure.
client_requirements: Simple npm-installable CLI/TypeScript library (`npm i -g @styfle/vgrok`), no TAP/TUN, no admin/root privileges on the client host itself. However, it additionally requires the Vercel CLI (or VERCEL_TEAM_ID/VERCEL_PROJECT_ID/VERCEL_TOKEN env vars) and a Vercel account/project link -- an external dependency beyond a plain binary install.
server_requirements: There is no self-hostable open-source 'server' at all -- vgrok's 'server' IS a Vercel Sandbox (a proprietary, metered Vercel product) spun up per tunnel; the repo only contains client-side TypeScript (`src/`) that talks to Vercel's infrastructure. We cannot host this ourselves; it fundamentally depends on Vercel's paid sandbox product and would tie our hosted service to a third-party vendor and its cost model.
server_language: N/A -- 'server' is Vercel's proprietary Sandbox product, not open-source code in this repo. Client library itself is TypeScript.
has_programmable_api: true (client-side only) -- TypeScript programmatic API exists (`import { client } from '@styfle/vgrok'; const tunnel = await client({ port, timeout })`), but this only drives Vercel's hosted sandbox infrastructure, not a self-hostable server/control-plane of our own.
viability_notes: Despite having a clean TypeScript client API, this is disqualifying: the 'server' side is entirely Vercel's proprietary Sandbox product (with Hobby-plan timeouts, single-region limits, and per-use costs), not open-source infrastructure we could self-host and expose via our own control plane.
